mechanicTruth: Heat, not cold, does most of the damage to a lead-acid battery: high underhood temperatures speed up evaporation and plate corrosion, so capacity drops through the warm months. The first cold morning only exposes the loss, because cold thickens the oil and leaves less usable capacity, which shows up as a slow crank.
selectedCaption: Everyone blames winter for this. Summer is what actually kills your battery. Heat cooks the acid and corrodes the plates all season, quietly — then one cool morning, there's nothing left to give. Slow crank. Dim headlights at idle. One jump start already. Most batteries last three to five years — heat cuts that shorter. Worth checking before it strands you.
voiceoverScript: Summer wears batteries down. Heat cooks the acid. Plates corrode, capacity drops. Cold only exposes it. Slow crank, worth checking.
